approachQuestion.prompt:
Packed Signal Equality

A packed signal is a read-only array of records [letter,count], where letter is a lowercase English letter and count is a positive integer. It represents count copies of letter, in record order. Adjacent records may use the same letter; the packing is not necessarily minimal. Given packed signals first and second, return whether their expanded character sequences are identical. Do not modify the records.

Constraints: 0 <= n=first.length, m=second.length <= 200000; 1 <= count <= 1000000000000. Expanded lengths and all count arithmetic fit signed 64-bit integers. Expansion is not supplied.

Example 1: first=[["a",3],["a",2],["b",1]], second=[["a",5],["b",1]] -> true.
Example 2: first=[["a",2],["b",1]], second=[["a",1],["b",2]] -> false.
Example 3: first=[], second=[] -> true.
constraints: Choose the most efficient valid approach for the entire stated input domain; accept equivalent optimal variants.

options.text: Keep a record index and remaining count for each signal. Require the current letters to match, subtract the smaller remaining count from both, and advance each exhausted record. Accept only when both signals end together.
options.feedback: Each equal-letter chunk matches exactly that many expanded positions. Consuming a partial record preserves the unmatched suffix without materializing it.

options.text: Copy each signal into a new list that merges adjacent equal-letter records, then compare those normalized lists exactly.
options.feedback: Normalization correctly gives a unique representation, but storing both normalized lists is unnecessary for a direct chunk comparison.

options.text: Accept only if the original record arrays have the same length and identical record pairs at every position.
options.feedback: [["a",2],["a",3]] and [["a",5]] expand identically despite different record arrays.

options.text: Sum the counts for each letter in each signal and accept if all 26 totals agree.
options.feedback: [["a",1],["b",1]] and [["b",1],["a",1]] have the same letter totals but different expanded order.

feedback.reason: Compare compressed streams by consuming the shorter remaining run without expanding or requiring normalized encoding.
details: Keep one current record and remaining count for each signal. Reject unequal current letters. Otherwise subtract the smaller remaining count from both; replace every exhausted record with its successor. Continue until a signal ends and accept only if both end together.

Subtract the smaller remaining run count from both signals. At least one record then ends, even when a record represents billions of characters. Joint exhaustion distinguishes equal prefixes from equal complete signals.

Accept only when both signals end together.”: Each equal-letter chunk matches exactly that many expanded positions. Consuming a partial record preserves the unmatched suffix without materializing it.

“Copy each signal into a new list that merges adjacent equal-letter records, then compare those normalized lists exactly.”: Normalization correctly gives a unique representation, but storing both normalized lists is unnecessary for a direct chunk comparison.
“Accept only if the original record arrays have the same length and identical record pairs at every position.”: [["a",2],["a",3]] and [["a",5]] expand identically despite different record arrays.
“Sum the counts for each letter in each signal and accept if all 26 totals agree.”: [["a",1],["b",1]] and [["b",1],["a",1]] have the same letter totals but different expanded order.

complexityQuestion.prompt: For the fixed method revealed after question 1, choose its tight worst-case time and auxiliary-space pair. Use a word-RAM model with constant-time indexed access and signed 64-bit arithmetic. Include all temporary buffers, input copies, and call frames; exclude supplied input and returned output. n and m count records, not expanded characters. Signed 64-bit count subtraction is constant time. The fixed method is iterative, expands no characters, allocates no record copy or work list, and uses no recursion, hashing, or amortized operations. E denotes the sum of the two expanded character lengths.
constraints: Analyze this fixed method regardless of your answer to question 1; choose the tightest pair.

options.text: O(n + m + 1) time, O(1) auxiliary space
O(n + m + 1) time, O(n + m + 1) auxiliary space

feedback.reason: Work follows compressed record counts rather than expanded lengths.
details: Every iteration consumes at least one whole record, giving at most n+m iterations regardless of huge represented counts. Equal signals with many records require reading their records. Only two indices, two 64-bit counts, and current letters are kept.

Use a word-RAM model with constant-time indexed access and signed 64-bit arithmetic. Include all temporary buffers, input copies, and call frames; exclude supplied input and returned output. n and m count records, not expanded characters. Signed 64-bit count subtraction is constant time. The fixed method is iterative, expands no characters, allocates no record copy or work list, and uses no recursion, hashing, or amortized operations.
“O(n + m + 1) time, O(n + m + 1) auxiliary space”: This adds normalized record lists that the fixed method avoids.
“O((n + 1)(m + 1)) time, O(1) auxiliary space”: Records are consumed rather than compared in every cross-pair.
“O(E + 1) time, O(1) auxiliary space”: Here E is the sum of expanded lengths. This is a loose bound for character-by-character expansion, not the tight record-based bound of the fixed method.
